paras: The East St. Louis school dispute of 1882 was a conflict in East St. Louis, Illinois, in September 1882, when Black children refused a separate school site were turned away from the white schools and street fights followed. The schools were closed on two successive days, and fights between white and Black children were reported before the dispute was said to have ended on September 13 with Black families accepting separate schools. Wire versions ran nationally under headlines such as "A War of Races" and "The Color Line."

During the summer vacation the East St. Louis School Board selected a site for a school building for Black children located between railroad tracks. Black residents objected to the location and threatened to send their children to school with white pupils.

When the schools opened on Monday, September 11, Black children applied for admission to the white schools and the principals refused them, after which the board closed the schools for the day. Several street fights occurred that night. On Tuesday the schools reopened, but few white children came while the Black children returned and were again refused; some teachers left, and the schools closed for the rest of the day.

The detailed dispatch reported fights between white and Black children that Tuesday morning, while a shorter brief said the street fights involved both children and parents. Another short dispatch said the schools had twice closed with "white children being afraid to go." No report names a participant, says which side began the fights, or describes any injury.

In the meantime the board had rented a building as a school for Black children, which families at first refused to use, "claiming the right to have them enrolled in the white schools." An Associated Press dispatch of September 13 reported that the excitement had subsided that day, Black families agreeing to send their children to the separate schools the board provided. No report of arrests or court action appears in the coverage.

Only white newspapers covered the dispute, mostly by reprinting two wire texts from September 12 and a short settlement notice from September 13. Because the detailed text carried a St. Louis dateline, the Savannah Morning News, the Richmond Dispatch and the Shenandoah Herald placed the events in St. Louis itself, and the Vermont Phoenix put East St. Louis in Missouri, while the Washington Evening Critic noted that the town lay across the river in Illinois. Headlines cast it as "A War of Races," a "School War" and, in Richmond, "The Negroes Defiant."

The Manitowoc Pilot wrote that the schools had been closed "rather than have them continue with negro children among the pupils." In an editorial, the Washington National Republican held that a dangerous site was proper ground for complaint and that excluding Black children without adequate separate schools was unjust, yet urged Black parents not to seek "white company" for its own sake. Several Midwestern weeklies ran the children-and-parents brief in their crime columns as late as September 22, and the Weekly Floridian printed the unresolved dispatch on October 3, after the settlement had been reported.

reader.title: East St. Louis school dispute of 1882
bases: A school-segregation dispute in which Black children were refused admission to white schools and street fights and fights between white and Black children followed, with no reported killing, injury or organized attack (A4, A20, A14).

Two differently worded dispatches, the short one (A1, A2) and the detailed one (A4, A7), agree on the refusals, the disputed site, the street fights and the closures, and a third brief adds parents' involvement (A20).

accounts.gist: The board built a school house for Black pupils, who objected to its location; street fights followed and the schools were twice closed, white children being afraid to go.

accounts.label: Detailed wire report
accounts.gist: Day-by-day account of refusals on Sept. 11 and 12, street fights the first night, fights between children the second morning, and Black families' refusal of a rented interim building.

accounts.label: Children-and-parents brief
accounts.gist: Schools closed because Black children were refused admission; street fights occurred between both the children and the parents.

accounts.label: AP settlement dispatch
accounts.gist: The excitement subsided Sept. 13 when Black families agreed to send their children to separate schools.

framing.detail: Most papers ran the wire text under heads such as 'A WAR OF RACES' and 'THE COLOR LINE', calling Black residents 'the negroes'.
The Richmond Dispatch headlined 'THE NEGROES DEFIANT' over the same dispatch.

The National Republican granted that a dangerous site was proper ground for complaint and that exclusion without adequate separate schools was unjust, but urged Black parents not to seek 'white company' as such.
The Manitowoc Pilot said the schools were closed 'rather than' continue with Black pupils.

conflicts.note: Identical wording shows one dispatch; the St. Louis dateline led some editors to drop 'East', and the Evening Critic explicitly placed the town in Illinois.
The Sept. 12 dispatch and explicit weekdays are the stronger evidence; the Waco date is a later re-dating.
